planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to morning sun; the multicolor variegation is most vivid on new growth in dappled light.

directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to morning sun, sheltered from the hottest afternoon exposure. Goshiki (Japanese for 'five colors') is a slow-growing, spiny-leaved evergreen shrub whose new growth emerges in a mottled blend of pink, cream, and bronze over dark green, settling into a creamy-mottled variegated pattern as the leaves mature — a striking, ever-changing foliage display that provides year-round color in a shaded border without relying on flowers. Its dense, holly-like, prickly foliage also gives it useful deer resistance and makes an attractive, low-maintenance foundation or accent shrub for shaded entries and woodland-edge plantings. Little pruning is needed given its slow growth rate; shape lightly if needed after the inconspicuous fall flowers finish.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil in partial shade to full sun.

directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil in partial shade to full sun. Fudingzhu is a Chinese tea olive selection bred for exceptionally heavy, repeat bloom — flowering several times a year rather than the one or two main flushes typical of standard tea olive — filling the garden with the intensely sweet, apricot-like fragrance for which the species is prized over a much longer season. Its more compact growth rate compared to seed-grown tea olive makes it a better fit for foundation plantings and smaller gardens where the species' eventual large size would be unwelcome. Plant it near a patio, walkway, or window where the fragrance can be enjoyed on its frequent bloom cycles; little pruning is needed beyond light shaping after flowering.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to morning sun.

directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to morning sun, sheltered from the hottest afternoon exposure. Variegatus is one of the oldest and most classic variegated false holly cultivars, its spiny, holly-like leaves crisply edged in creamy white around a dark green center, providing bright, reliable, year-round contrast in a shaded border without depending on bloom for interest. Tiny, sweetly fragrant white flowers appear tucked among the leaves in fall, easy to miss visually but noticeable by scent alone. Its dense, evergreen, deer-resistant foliage makes it a durable choice for shaded foundation plantings, informal hedges, and screens; little pruning is needed beyond light shaping after fall bloom.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun. John Nelson is a selected cleyera cultivar valued for denser branching and more compact, uniform growth than seed-grown plants, with the same glossy, oval, dark-green leaves that emerge bronze-red on new growth and small, fragrant, creamy flowers in summer followed by red berries. Its improved density makes it a stronger choice for screening and hedging than straight-species cleyera, while retaining the shade tolerance that makes the species valuable as an alternative to photinia or ligustrum in partly shaded Gulf Coast landscapes. It requires little pruning to hold an attractive form and is largely untroubled by pests or disease.

planting.note: Plant container specimens in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade in spring or fall.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade; like the species, Compacta tolerates shade, clay soil, drought, and salt spray far better than most conifers. This dwarf selection stays a fraction of the size of standard yew podocarpus, forming a dense, rounded shrub of the same long, flat, dark-green, yew-like leaves without the eventual height of the straight species, making it a better fit for foundation plantings and low hedges where full-size podocarpus would need constant shearing to control. Slow-growing and low-maintenance, it is virtually pest-free in Gulf Coast conditions and holds its neat form with minimal pruning.
sources: Clemson Cooperative Extension Home & Garden Information Center

planting.note: Plant container specimens in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade in spring or fall; Maki is commonly clipped as a hedge or espalier.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade. Maki is a shorter, denser, more shrubby form of yew podocarpus than the columnar tree form, with narrower, shorter needle-like leaves densely packed on upright stems, widely used throughout the Gulf South as a clipped hedge, foundation shrub, or trained espalier. Like the species, it tolerates significant shade, clay soil, salt spray, and drought far better than most needled evergreens, and it accepts frequent shearing well, holding a crisp, formal shape when clipped regularly or growing more loosely and naturally if left alone. Its small, fleshy, red-purple fruit receptacles are attractive to birds; it is essentially pest-free in Gulf Coast landscapes.
sources: Clemson Cooperative Extension Home & Garden Information Center

common_name: Queen Mum Agapanthus (Giant Bicolor White-and-Blue Lily of the Nile)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; like other agapanthus, Queen Mum blooms most heavily when slightly root-bound, so avoid dividing too often.

directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Queen Mum is one of the largest-flowered agapanthus cultivars grown, producing huge, rounded flower heads up to 10 inches across on tall, sturdy scapes well above the strap-like evergreen foliage. Each individual flower is a striking bicolor — white with a fine blue picotee edge and blue veining — giving the giant flower heads a frosted, two-toned effect distinct from the solid blue or solid white agapanthus cultivars more commonly seen. Its bold scale makes it a strong specimen or accent plant rather than a mass groundcover choice. Drought-tolerant once established; divide congested clumps only every 5–7 years, since flowering is heaviest when the roots are somewhat crowded.

common_name: Silver Lace Society Garlic (Variegated Society Garlic)

planting.note: Plant rhizome clumps in early spring in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; in zone 7 provide heavy mulch for winter protection, as plants can be damaged below 20°F.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; this South African native is extremely drought-tolerant once established and thrives in zone 9–10 gardens. Silver Lace is a variegated society garlic selection, its strap-like leaves crisply edged in creamy white, adding season-long foliage interest to the near-year-round clusters of lavender, garlic-scented flowers typical of the species. Like the plain green form, leaves and flowers carry a mild garlic flavor without lingering breath and make a useful, ornamental garlic substitute in the kitchen, while the flowers reliably draw bees and small pollinators. Divide clumps every 3–4 years in spring to maintain vigor and clean variegation.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun.

directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; Caramel bears unusual soft apricot-caramel flowers that deepen slightly toward the center, a warmer, more muted tone than the bright golden-yellow typical of most coreopsis cultivars, held above a compact, tidy mound of narrow foliage. It flowers heavily from early summer into fall and draws bees and small pollinators, tolerating heat, humidity, and poor soil well once established. Shear the plant back by about a third after the first flush of bloom to encourage a fresh round of flowers and keep the habit tidy; divide congested clumps every few years in spring if the center begins to thin.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun.

directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; Full Moon produces some of the largest individual flowers of any coreopsis cultivar, broad, pale creamy-yellow blooms up to 3 inches across held well above a full, vigorous clump of narrow foliage, giving it a bolder presence in the border than the smaller-flowered threadleaf types. It blooms heavily from early summer into fall and draws bees and small pollinators, tolerating heat and humidity well once established. Shear the plant back by about a third after the first flush of bloom to encourage continued flowering, and divide congested clumps every few years in spring if the center begins to thin.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun.

directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; Summer Nights bears vivid, saturated magenta-pink petals held outward to slightly downward around a prominent dark orange-brown cone, on a compact, sturdy, well-branched plant that produces far more flowers per stem than older coneflower selections. Its intense color and heavy bloom make it a strong pollinator draw through summer, and its heat and drought tolerance suit it well to a Gulf South perennial border once established. Deadhead spent flowers to prolong bloom, or leave some seed heads standing into fall and winter to feed goldfinches. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring if flowering starts to decline.
